design_detail: Theoretical narrative review, the lead article of a Drug and Alcohol Dependence supplement (vol. 123, Suppl. 1), contrasting the 'gateway hypothesis' (a sequence of first use from tobacco or alcohol to cannabis to other illicit drugs) with the concept of a common liability to addiction (a single latent, largely heritable trait behind the risk of all drug addictions). It draws on genetic, psychometric, neurobiological, epidemiological and evolutionary arguments and ends with untested evolutionary hypotheses. No search strategy, selection criteria, appraisal or synthesis of data; one conceptual figure; no tables.
can_establish: The case made by the group that developed the common-liability concept and its measurement for why the usual order of first drug use need not reflect causal stages, and pointers to the twin, psychometric, cross-national and genetic studies it cites in support.
cannot_establish: Whether one drug's use raises the risk of using another, or by how much (no new data, no systematic search, no appraisal of the cited studies); whether common liability explains the order of initiation better than a causal or an availability explanation (designs that found associations surviving familial control are not discussed); any heritability figure, population or era (none is given); or anything about the evolutionary hypotheses, which are offered as proposals.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: no search or selection method is described; the authors chose the literature.
sample.selection_effects: The cited evidence for common liability is drawn largely from twin and psychometric studies, about a fifth of all references include one of the authors, and the central developmental evidence (the transmissible liability index, pubertal maturation and deviant peers) is the group's own. Studies that found the association between early cannabis use and later drug use surviving co-twin control or extensive adjustment, named in this round's reading list (Lynskey et al., 2003; Fergusson et al., 2006), are not cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The paper treats the order of first use of tobacco or alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs as the gateway 'exposure', and the latent common liability, indexed by the group's transmissible liability index (TLI) built from psychological indicators measured before drug use, as the alternative.
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the paper: co-occurrence of use and of use disorders across drugs, explained by a shared liability.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the paper's argument is that pre-drug characteristics (behavioural disinhibition, externalizing problems, pubertal timing) carry much of the risk, but it reports no data of its own on them.

outcomes.operationalization: Addiction is treated as compulsive drug seeking and use, distinguished from physiological dependence; liability is a latent quantitative trait with a diagnostic threshold, below which it is 'propensity' and above which 'severity' (Section 3.1).

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported. The few numbers are cited from other sources: from the 2007 US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, lifetime use among people aged 18–49 of marijuana by about half, cigarettes by 70% and alcohol by 90%, and cocaine by almost a quarter of those aged 35–49 (Section 3.2.2, 2nd paragraph); from Degenhardt et al. (2010), cannabis use by 4.5% and other illicit drug use by 4.8% of 18–29-year-olds in Japan, where 83.2% of people who used other illicit drugs had not used cannabis first (Section 2, 6th paragraph; see reporting issues). Genetic statements (moderate to high heritability; little drug-specific genetic variance; heritability rising with age) carry no estimates. The review also says that more than 50% of people with an addiction have other psychopathology, citing Regier et al. (1990), an Epidemiologic Catchment Area report by its reference title, with no population or years given; its wording names the people by a label the site does not use (3.4.4, 8th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is selected to support one side; the qualifications in the gateway literature are quoted as evasions rather than weighed, and evidence of residual associations after familial control is not discussed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An argued critique of the gateway concept (stages defined circularly, frequent reversals of the order, dependence of the order on how common each drug is, no mechanism separate from drug use itself) and a case for a common liability resting on cited twin evidence of shared genetic risk across drug use disorders, psychometric evidence that symptoms for different drugs lie on one dimension, and the group's own developmental studies; no new data and no appraisal of the cited studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says initiation sequencing is 'variable and opportunistic rather than uniform and developmentally deterministic', and the Conclusions call common liability 'parsimonious and empirically proven' and the gateway hypothesis 'redundant', possibly hindering research and intervention. Gaps: (1) 'empirically proven' is stated for a latent construct supported by correlational twin and psychometric evidence that the paper summarizes without estimates or appraisal; (2) the paper treats common liability and gateway effects as mutually exclusive, but a shared liability does not rule out an additional causal effect of earlier use, and the designs that test this (co-twin control, cohorts with extensive adjustment) are not discussed; (3) the claim that causality is 'readily refuted' by atypical sequences misreads a probabilistic claim, since a drug can raise the risk of using another without the order being invariant; (4) the gateway concept is presented in its deterministic form while its proponents' stated qualifications are dismissed as hedging; (5) the closing statement that 'the papers in this special issue' support the conclusion names none of them.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the origin of the gateway sequence criticised here.
Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a common-factor model reproduces the gateway pattern; cited as support for common liability and opportunity.
Lynskey et al.: co-twin control study of early cannabis use and later drug use, named in this round's reading list among designs that kept an association after adjustment; not cited by this review.
Tarter et al. (the review's own group): predictors of marijuana use before and after licit drug use; cited as evidence of reversals of the sequence.
Degenhardt et al., WHO World Mental Health Surveys: the order of first use varies with each drug's prevalence across 17 countries; cited here for the Japan figures (see reporting issues).

Irons, Iacono & McGue (Iacono is a co-author of this review), Minnesota twins (read in this round): drinking by 14 associated with more drug classes used at 24 within MZ pairs discordant for early drinking, which a liability shared by co-twins cannot by itself produce.

replication.where_it_stands: A position paper by the main proponents of common liability and the reading list's liability source on the gateway question. Its critique of the gateway concept is reasonable as argument, but it does not engage the designs that found associations persisting after control for familial factors, and later co-twin evidence on early drinking (Irons et al., 2015) found within-MZ-pair associations with later drug use. The reading list notes that no study separates the causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design; the two explanations may both hold.

funding.funder: Role of funding source, as printed: NIDA had no role in the analysis, preparation and writing of the report or in the decision to submit it. No grant numbers are given in the author manuscript; a disclaimer states that the views are the authors' and not those of NIDA or any sponsoring organization.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Pittsburgh (most, including the first author), Rockefeller University, Johns Hopkins, the University of Minnesota, Washington University and Virginia Commonwealth University, and one from NIDA's Division of Epidemiology, Services and Prevention Research. The review is the lead article of a special issue and promotes its authors' concept and instrument (the transmissible liability index); recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that separates the three explanations in one design: for example a genetically informative cohort with drug use recorded as it happens, measuring liability before any use, local availability of each drug, and the order of first use, with MZ twins discordant for early cannabis use, and testing whether early use of one drug predicts later use of another beyond both shared liability and opportunity.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

No appraisal: cited findings are stated as established, including figures that rest on a handful of respondents (the Japan figures) and a claim of a negligible true association between cannabis and other drug use attributed to Earleywine (2002) without data.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 30 of the 145 references (21%) include one of the authors (one of them, Walden et al., 2004, with Iacono's name printed as 'Lacono'), and the developmental and measurement evidence for common liability (transmissible liability index, pubertal maturation, deviant peers) is the group's own; the genetic-correlation evidence comes mostly from other groups.

The evolutionary section is presented as proposals and testable hypotheses, but it runs on from the evidence without a clear break, uses value-laden groupings (it lists homosexuality with suicide and celibacy among behaviours said to need a Darwinian explanation), and the Conclusions call common liability empirically proven.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal gateway effect
domains.note: Evidence that associations between earlier and later drug use survive co-twin control or extensive adjustment is not cited; the gateway concept is presented in its strongest deterministic form.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This is an advocacy review by the proponents of one explanation, without search or appraisal and with the opposing evidence largely absent. It may be cited for the argument against reading the order of first use as causal stages, for its definitions of common liability, and as a pointer to the twin and psychometric studies it relies on (which must be read themselves); not for the size of any genetic or gateway effect, for heritability figures, or for the claim that common liability is proven.

key_findings.finding: The authors define the gateway hypothesis as a sequence of first use from tobacco or alcohol to cannabis to other illicit drugs, and common liability as a non-specific liability to all drug addictions regardless of the order of initiation; they note that the gateway hypothesis addresses only initiation, not the development of use disorders.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 6th paragraph; 2. Gateway hypothesis, 1st and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that gateway 'stages' are defined circularly (the stage is identified by the drug and the drug by the stage), that no mechanism separate from drug use is specified, and that its proponents avoid explicit causal claims while implying that earlier drugs are required for progression.

Reversals of the sequence are described as common, citing studies in which a substantial share of people started with illicit drugs or used other drugs before cannabis, and the cross-national WHO surveys (Degenhardt et al., 2010) for Japan, where cannabis was used by 4.5% and other illicit drugs by 4.8% of 18–29-year-olds and 83.2% of people who used other illicit drugs had not used cannabis first.
key_findings.note: The Japan figures combine age groups and rest on very few respondents in the source (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Against a gateway role of alcohol and tobacco the authors cite a study titled in the reference list as a Mendelian-randomization test, in which aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency was related to lower rates of drinking but did not predict lower rates of other drug use (Irons et al., 2007), and a school-based randomized prevention trial (by its reference title) after which early protection against or delays in tobacco onset did not reduce later involvement with cannabis or other illegal drugs (Furr-Holden et al., 2004); no numbers are given.

Cited evidence for a common liability: high genetic correlations between liabilities to different drug addictions with virtually no drug-specific genetic variance (Kendler et al., 2003), apart from a licit versus illicit grouping (Kendler et al., 2007); symptoms of different drug use disorders lying on one dimension; and a statistical model in which correlations of cannabis and other drug use are accounted for by common liability and opportunity (Morral et al., 2002). No estimates, populations or eras are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.1 Empirical support for the common addiction liability concept; 1. Introduction, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state, citing twin studies, that variation in starting drug use owes much to shared and non-shared environment, whereas variation in use disorders is predominantly genetic with no detectable shared-environment effect, and that heritability grows with age (Hicks et al., 2007); when the review cites Hicks et al. (2007) again, it is for a combined antisocial-behaviour and drug-dependence construct whose heritability grows with age "at least in males"; no figures or samples are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 3.4.4 Drug abuse and (anti)social behavior, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' transmissible liability index, built from psychological indicators measured before drug use, was higher in boys who later developed cannabis use disorder than in boys who used cannabis without developing it (Kirisci et al., 2009, the authors' own study); no numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that any sensitization by cannabis to other drugs would be shared by all drugs and so could not single out cannabis as a gateway, and that the probability of starting with a given drug follows its prevalence and availability, making the sequence opportunistic.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The only data the review cites against cannabis sensitization is Ellgren et al. (2004) (3.2.2, 6th paragraph). The review does not say what kind of study it was; its reference title (dopamine levels and behaviour after cannabinoid exposure during adolescence, in a pharmacology journal) describes an experiment that reads as an animal study, so any use of the point must check that paper and label it.

key_findings.finding: On language, the authors argue that any new label for addiction will acquire the negative connotations of the old ones because illicit behaviour evokes negative reactions, and that addiction, though a disorder, results from voluntary norm-violating behaviour and is "subject to moral judgment regardless of the term used".
key_findings.note: An opinion, with no data; relevant to the encyclopedia's question on words and stigma as an example of one position.

key_findings.finding: The evolutionary section proposes, as hypotheses, that drugs act on an evolved common reward metric as a false fitness signal, and that people with a low amplitude of affective states in safe modern environments seek larger changes, including through drug use and risky or antisocial behaviour.
key_findings.locator: 3.4.2 Common metric system; 3.4.3 The amplitude of affective states (AAS) hypothesis

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions call common liability parsimonious and empirically proven, the gateway hypothesis redundant and of uncertain utility, and warn that presenting the sequence as a theory may be misread causally and hinder research and intervention.

The review cites an association of AVPR1A gene variants with the risk for addiction in men but not in women (Maher et al., 2011, a study with several of the review's authors), reported as mediated by indicators of the quality of mates' relationships, with the associated alleles flipping between samples; one cited study, no numbers.
key_findings.note: A single cited study of a sex difference; for the round's questions on women and men it is a pointer only, to be read in the original.

reporting_issues.issue: The Japan example pairs prevalences for 18–29-year-olds (cannabis 4.5%, other illicit drugs 4.8%) with the all-ages proportion of people using other illicit drugs who had not used cannabis first (83.2%). In the source (Degenhardt et al., 2010, read in this round), the prevalences rest on 4 respondents each, the 83.2% on about 13 of 16 respondents of all ages, and the 18–29 proportion is 77.3% with a standard error of 52.4 points. The Japanese survey sampled people aged 20 and over in four metropolitan areas (Degenhardt et al., 2010, Table 1), so the '18–29' band is 20–29 there and the figures are not national.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2. Gateway hypothesis, 6th paragraph; compare sc_degenhardt_2010a (Tables 2 and 4 of that paper)
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure presented as 'a staggering 83.2%' is an all-ages estimate from a handful of people; it illustrates that the order can differ where cannabis is rare, but cannot carry weight as a population estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The 6th paragraph of section 3.4.4 (the paragraph on Moffitt, 1993) refers to 'the discussed paper's Fig. 3', but this paper has only one figure; the reference appears to be to a figure in Moffitt (1993), discussed in the preceding sentences.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 3.4.4 Drug abuse and (anti)social behavior, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point about a continuous age-of-onset distribution cannot be checked in this paper.
